<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par109 />{{GHGmargin-letter|109|g}}
Rem. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=35|verse=21}} a negative final clause with {{GHGheb|text=וְאַל־}} is dependent on an imperative, ''forbear from'' (meddling with) ''God''... ''that he destroy thee not''. As a rule, however, negative final clauses are attached to the principal sentence by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} and a following imperfect; so after an imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=44|hidebook=1}}; after a jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=9}}; after a perfect consec., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=35}}, 43, 30:12, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=18|verse=5}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with an imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=18|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=17|verse=17}} ''neither shall he multiply wives unto himself'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ}}) ''that his heart turn not away''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=11|verse=21}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} with jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=43|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=16|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=24|hidebook=1}} f.; after the asseverative {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with the impft., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=23}}; even after a simple imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=4}} ''with nails''... ''they fasten it'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יָפִיק}}) ''that it move not''; after a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|h}}
(''b'') Frequently in conditional sentences (as in Arabic), either in the protasis or in the apodosis, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=יִתְאָו|translate=should he desire}}... ''then''...; 104:20 {{GHGheb|text=תָּ֫שֶׁת... וִיהִי|translate=if thou makest darkness, then it is night}}; so also in the protasis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=15|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְיַ֫עַל}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=29}}; in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=7|verse=9}} ''then will it'' (not, ''then shall it'') ''become a serpent''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=9}} after an imperat. in the protasis; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=28|hidebook=1}}. In a negative apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=12}} ({{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־תֹסֵף}}, but see above, ''d''). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־יֽוֹשִׁעֵךְ}} (''if the Lord do not help thee'', &c.) is to be explained as a jussive in a negative protasis.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|i}}
Rem. Undoubtedly this use of the jussive (in conditional sentences) is based on its original ''voluntative'' meaning; let something be so and so, then this or that must happen as a consequence. Certain other examples of the {{GHGterm|jussive}}, however, show that in the consciousness of the language the ''voluntative'' has in such cases become weakened almost to a ''potential'' mood, and hence the {{GHGterm|jussive}} serves to express facts which may happen ''contingently'', or may be expected, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=19}} ({{GHGheb|text=מַה־יֹּסֵף}}, but cf. above, ''d''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=33}} ''there is no daysman betwixt us, that might lay'' ({{GHGheb|text=יָשֵׁת}}, hence plainly a ''subjunctive=qui ponat''; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=וִֽיכַזֵּב|translate=that he should lie}} is probably intended as a jussive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=14}}; so after interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=11}} ''who is the wise man'', {{GHGheb|text=וְיָבֵן|translate=qui intelligat hoc}}?; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=10}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|k}}
Moreover, in not a few cases, the jussive is used, without any collateral sense, for the ordinary imperfect form, and this occurs not alone in forms, which may arise from a misunderstanding of the defective writing, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=21}}, 36, 32:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=21|verse=2|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} ({{GHGheb|text=מַה־יָּ֫גֶל}}, {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=יָגִיל}}), 25:9, 47:4, 90:3, 91:4, 107:29, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=37|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=12|verse=6}} (verse 7 {{GHGheb|text=יָשֹׁב}}, but immediately afterwards {{GHGheb|text=תָּשׁוּב}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=12}}, —but also in shortened forms, such as {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=17}} (Sam. {{GHGheb|text=יִהְיֶה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=9|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=16}} f. (after other jussives), 104:31, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, 26, 28, 27:8, 33:21, 34:37, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=4}}. This use of the jussive can hardly be due merely to poetic licence, but is rather to be explained on rhythmical grounds. In all the above-cited examples, in fact, the jussive stands at the beginning of the sentence (and hence removed as far as possible from the principal tone), in others it is immediately before the principal pause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=19|hidebook=1}}), or actually ''in'' pause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=9}}, 11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=50}}), and is then a simply rhythmical shortening due to the strong influence of the tone. Moreover, since the jussive in numerous cases is not distinguished in form from the imperfect ({{GHGpar|48|g}}), it is frequently doubtful which of the two the writer intended. This especially applies to those cases, in which a ''subjunctive'' is to be expressed by one or other of the forms (cf. {{GHGpar|107|k}} and ''m''–''x'').<section end=par109 /><noinclude>
